evidence.claim: A gentle climb from North Park gives way to the steep Poudre descent.
evidence.quote: The pass has a mild approach from the West where the road rises out of the broad North Park area, and is steep from the East where the road climbs from Fort Collins up the narrow Poudre River valley.

evidence.claim: From the open basin of North Park, Highway 14 climbs gently toward Cameron Pass before descending steeply into the narrow Poudre River valley.
evidence.quote: The pass has a mild approach from the West where the road rises out of the broad North Park area, and is steep from the East where the road climbs from Fort Collins up the narrow Poudre River valley.

evidence.claim: The Colorado Department of Transportation includes Cache la Poudre–North Park in its Scenic & Historic Byways program and gives the drive between Walden and Fort Collins as 101 miles and three hours.
evidence.quote: Cache la Poudre - North Park Length: 101 miles Driving time: 3 hours This byway links Fort Collins with Walden

evidence.claim: The Colorado Department of Transportation includes Cache la Poudre–North Park in its Scenic & Historic Byways program
evidence.quote: Colorado Scenic & Historic Byways

evidence.claim: Its description emphasizes the river canyon and the glaciated mountains and evergreen thickets at Colorado State Forest.
evidence.quote: At 10,276-foot Cameron Pass, the highway intersects Colorado State Forest, a 70,000-acre preserve of glaciated mountains and evergreen thickets.

evidence.claim: Highway 14 is two lanes except for sections near Fort Collins.
evidence.quote: The highway is two-lane along its entire route, except for portions near Fort Collins where it is concurrent with U.S. Highway 287, and east of Fort Collins near its interchange with Interstate 25.

evidence.claim: Railroad companies surveyed the canyon in the early 1880s, including rivals Union Pacific and Chicago, Burlington and Quincy. No railroad followed; a road was built through the narrows in the 1920s.
evidence.quote: In the early 1880s, the canyon was surveyed for a railroad by archrivals, the Union Pacific Railroad and the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad, with the intention of completing a transcontinental line through the Rockies. The canyon was never the site of a railroad, however, during the 1920s a road was constructed through the narrows.

evidence.claim: Baldwin Tunnel began as a single-lane rock tunnel in 1916. It was widened to two lanes in 1951, before the highway’s paving was complete.
evidence.quote: Baldwin Tunnel is an unlined hard rock tunnel at milepost 107.3.  Originally completed in 1916 as only one lane wide, it was widened to two lanes in 1951.

evidence.claim: Highway 14 was fully paved by 1963.
evidence.quote: The entire route was paved by 1963

evidence.claim: Starting at Walden, follow the route southeast through Gould along the Michigan River valley to Cameron Pass.
evidence.quote: first going northeast to Walden, then southeast through Gould along the valley of the Michigan River. It then transverses along the southern end of the Medicine Bow Mountains at Cameron Pass

evidence.claim: Beyond the pass, the highway descends beside Joe Wright Creek to Chambers Lake, then follows the Cache la Poudre through its canyon.
evidence.quote: It then descends through the pass to the northwest along the valley of Joe Wright Creek to Chambers Lake, traveling through the mountains along the valley of the Cache la Poudre River and passing through the Poudre Canyon.

evidence.claim: At Teds Place, it joins US 287 southbound for Fort Collins.
evidence.quote: It joins U.S. Highway 287 southbound at Teds Place, a longtime local landmark just east of the mouth of the Poudre Canyon. It is concurrent with U.S. Route 287 southward to Fort Collins

evidence.claim: Wetlands, pine forest, aspen groves and sagebrush share the valley at Gould, between Owl Mountain and Gould Mountain.
evidence.quote: The community is situated in the valley of the Middle Fork of the Michigan River between Owl Mountain and Gould Mountain. The landscape is a patchwork of wetlands, pine forest, aspen groves, and sagebrush.

evidence.claim: Timber shaped the town at the turn of the twentieth century. In 1939, Gould and the Bockman Lumber Camp built simple log cabin schools.
evidence.quote: Life at the turn of the 20th century was centered on the timber industry.  In 1939 the town of Gould and the Bockman Lumber Camp built simple log cabin schools.

evidence.claim: In the 1950s, Colorado State Forest headquarters were built on the grounds of a former fish hatchery.
evidence.quote: In the 1950s the Colorado State Forest was created and the headquarters were built on the grounds of a former fish hatchery.

evidence.claim: The Moose Visitor Center stands on US 14, one mile east of Gould.
evidence.quote: Moose Visitor Center - State Forest State Park US Hwy 14 (1 mile east of Gould)

evidence.claim: Gould lies southeast of Walden on Highway 14, in the valley of the Middle Fork of the Michigan River.
evidence.quote: The community is located on State Highway 14, southeast of Walden in North Park. The community is situated in the valley of the Middle Fork of the Michigan River

evidence.claim: Gould’s valley includes wetlands, pine forest, aspen groves and sagebrush.
evidence.quote: The landscape is a patchwork of wetlands, pine forest, aspen groves, and sagebrush.

evidence.claim: Cameron Pass occupies a gap between the Medicine Bow and Never Summer mountains at 10,276 feet.
evidence.quote: Cameron Pass (elevation 10,276 ft; 3,132 m) is a mountain pass in north-central Colorado in the Rocky Mountains of the western United States. The pass is a gap between the south end of the Medicine Bow Mountains and the north end of the Never Summer Mountains.

evidence.claim: Named in 1870 for Robert Cameron, a former Union general and founder of the Fort Collins Agricultural Colony, it drew repeated railroad surveys.
evidence.quote: The pass was named for Robert Cameron, the founder of the Fort Collins Agricultural Colony and former Union general, in 1870. The pass was surveyed several times for railroads

evidence.claim: Union Pacific considered it for a route through the Rockies, but no railroad crossed the pass.
evidence.quote: including once by the Union Pacific Railroad as a possible route for a line through the Rockies. However, no railroad was ever built over the pass.

evidence.claim: Highway 14 now uses the gap to connect Fort Collins with Walden in North Park.
evidence.quote: The pass provides the most convenient route between Fort Collins and Walden in North Park, using State Highway 14.

evidence.claim: Water drains toward different branches of the Platte: Joe Wright Creek feeds the South Platte basin, while the Michigan River feeds the North Platte.
evidence.quote: The pass is drained on the north side by a tributary of the Cache la Poudre River, Joe Wright Creek, in the basin of the South Platte River. It is drained on the south side by the Michigan River, a tributary of the North Platte River in North Park.

evidence.claim: Cameron Pass usually remains open year-round, but receives heavy winter snow and is prone to avalanches.
evidence.quote: The pass receives much snow during the winter months and is prone to avalanches, but it usually remains open all-year round.

evidence.claim: Rustic stands beside Highway 14 and the Cache la Poudre River.
evidence.quote: Rustic is located on State Highway 14 and the Cache La Poudre River

evidence.claim: S. B. Stewart built the Rustic Hotel here in 1881; it soon became a summer tourist resort. The town was established the following year.
evidence.quote:
In 1881, S.B. Stewart built the Rustic Hotel at this location.  It soon became a popular summer tourist resort.
The town of Rustic was established in 1882.

evidence.claim: The hotel burned in 2008.
evidence.quote: Rustic was home to the Rustic Hotel, which was established in 1881 and burned down in 2008.

evidence.claim: Downstream, fishing and hunting resort cabins occur along the canyon, where some cabins are occupied only seasonally.
evidence.quote: Most of the habitation is the form of small cabins, some of which are inhabited only during season. Resort cabin communities for fishing and hunting are found sporadically along the canyon downstream from Rustic

flags: Rustic is retained as a town story, not a hotel recommendation; its hotel burned in 2008. The short moment reflects limited town evidence.
Current year-round opening language was too absolute: the pass source says usually. No live road status is available; practical checked date records cache review only.
River-name story omitted because the Laporte cache calls it legend while the river cache states it as fact. No other current claims were dropped for lack of cache support.
National Forest Scenic Byway designation is not established by the cached CDOT text; only its Colorado program context is used.
